result:
The library at the end of the world keeps no catalog. Books arrive the way weather does—unannounced, rearranging the air. Yesterday a slim volume appeared on the windowsill, its spine the color of a bruise just beginning to fade. When I opened it, the pages were blank except for a single sentence written in the margin of the last leaf: “You were here before the building was.”

I closed it and set it back. Outside, the sea had pulled so far away that the wet sand looked like a second sky. Gulls stood in the shallows arguing over nothing. I thought about the sentence for a long time, turning it the way you turn a smooth stone in your pocket until the heat of your hand becomes part of its shape.

Most days I reshelve what I can. A treatise on the migration of shadows. A cookbook whose recipes all begin with “First, forgive the onion.” A children’s atlas in which every country is labeled only with the name of its most famous lost thing. None of them stay where I put them. By morning they have drifted, the way conversations drift when no one is performing.

Sometimes a reader comes. They never ask for anything specific. They stand in the doorway until their eyes adjust, then wander until a book chooses them. I have watched a woman laugh so hard at a page that she had to sit on the floor. I have watched a man read three lines, close the book gently, and leave it on the chair as if it were a sleeping animal he didn’t want to wake. Neither of them spoke to me. Speech feels optional here, like shoes.

Tonight the tide is returning. I can hear it testing the lower steps, polite but insistent. The bruise-colored book is gone from the sill; in its place is a single feather, barred gray and white, still warm. I don’t know which bird left it or whether the book became the feather or the feather reminded the book it had somewhere else to be. Both explanations feel equally true, which is the only kind of truth the library seems interested in keeping.

I think I’ll leave the feather where it is. Tomorrow, or the day after, something else will arrive that needs the space. Until then the room is quiet enough to hear the faint, continuous sound of pages turning themselves, somewhere just out of sight, in a language no one has to translate.
